gw_in_sstp.revocation_note: The script turns off server certificate revocation checks for SSTP (NoCertRevocationCheck=1): the server’s self-signed certificate has no revocation list. Windows has no such setting per connection — it applies to all SSTP connections on this computer.
gw_in_sstp.domain_note: The server certificate is Let’s Encrypt for {domain}: the client verifies it on its own, no fingerprint to compare. Use exactly this domain as the server address (it must match the name in the certificate).
gw_in_sstp.err.no_cert: The SSTP certificate isn’t created yet: kaskadctl gw apply.
gw_in_sstp.self_signed: The server’s certificate is self-signed: compare the fingerprint on the first connection.
gw_in_sstp.cert_trust: Add it to trusted certificates so the client verifies the server.
gw_in_sstp.port_hint: If Windows doesn’t accept the address with port {port}, connect over IKEv2.
gw_in_sstp.ros_no_verify_le: The script doesn’t verify the certificate (verify-server-certificate=no); the server has a Let’s Encrypt certificate — you can turn verification on if RouterOS trusts the built-in root certificates.
gw_in_sstp.ros_no_verify_self: The script doesn’t verify the certificate (verify-server-certificate=no); to verify, import kaskad-sstp.crt into /certificate and set verify-server-certificate=yes.
gw_in_sstp.linux_pkg: Package sstp-client. The login and password are only in {file} (mode 600): never on the command line or in the shell history.
gw_in_sstp.linux_route: Add the route through the tunnel yourself (ip route) or use NetworkManager-sstp.
gw_in_sstp.rec.pppd: SSTP — login and password for pppd
gw_in_sstp.pppd_note: The file holds the password: install it with the command above (mode 600, owner root) and keep no copies.
gw_in_sstp.android: Open SSTP Client (Google Play, F-Droid): server {host}, port {port}, login and password{trust}.
